title: US Carrier Crew Crisis Deepens as Sailors Reportedly Try to Jump Ship, Oman Oil Spill Reaches Coastline, Romania Shuts Nuclear Plant Over Record-Low Danube
subhead: Allegations of food and water shortages aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln after 250-plus days at sea trigger a Senate inquiry and pressure the White House over the Iran war, while a 2,000-sq-km oil slick reaches Oman's shore and record-low European rivers force Romania to take its only nuclear plant offline.

sections.heading: USS Abraham Lincoln Crew Conditions Trigger Senate Pressure Over Iran War
sections.body:
Thousands of sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln have reportedly endured food shortages, broken plumbing and exhaustion after more than 250 days at sea, with military news outlets reporting that some have attempted to jump overboard, according to the BBC. The carrier left California in November for the South China Sea and was sent to the Middle East ahead of the US attacks on Iran in February; a deployment originally set to end in May has been repeatedly extended with no return date announced.

Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal listed the reported hardships in a letter to Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, citing 'shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in the mail system'. Blumenthal asked whether the Navy 'can sustain the operational tempo now being demanded of its carrier force', and fellow Democrat Ruben Gallego called for a congressional delegation to board the ship. Hegseth on Thursday dismissed the reports as 'completely misrepresented'. The BBC reported the US is preparing to replace the Lincoln with the USS George Washington as part of a scheduled rotation.
sections.whyItMatters: A crew-welfare crisis on the flagship carrier of the Iran campaign gives Congress a direct line of attack on the war's human cost, and publicly questions whether the US Navy can sustain the pace Washington is demanding of it.

sections.heading: Oman Oil Spill Reaches Coastline After Weeks of Unchecked Leak
sections.body:
A vast oil slick from the tanker Caroline Bezengi reached Oman's coastline on Wednesday, its environment agency said, with satellite imagery reviewed by Reuters showing the spill now covers more than 2,000 square kilometres. Oil has been leaking from the vessel since it ran aground off the Omani town of Sharbithat after reporting a suspected explosion on June 8 while en route from Russia to India; Reuters reported it was carrying an estimated 800,000 barrels of sanctioned oil.

The Oman News Agency quoted the environment authority saying a coastal stretch of up to 40km near Ras Madrakah is expected to be affected, with the southern beaches of Masirah Island potentially contaminated within hours. The slick is concentrated around the Hallaniyat Archipelago, where a marine reserve protecting rare sea turtles was established last year. Oil spill specialist John Amos called it potentially one of the world's worst spills in years, and the UN's International Maritime Organization said it was 'closely monitoring' the leak.
sections.whyItMatters: A sanctioned-oil spill spreading largely unchecked for weeks off the Arabian Sea coast shows how wartime sanctions enforcement and maritime disruption are compounding into an environmental disaster with real regional consequences.

sections.heading: Romania Takes Its Only Nuclear Plant Offline as the Danube Hits a 30-Year Low
sections.body:
Romania shut down the second reactor at Cernavodă, its only nuclear power station, because of extremely low water levels in the Danube caused by prolonged heat across much of Europe, according to the BBC. The two 706-megawatt reactors produce about 20% of Romania's electricity, and plant director Romeo Urjan told AFP the plant is not expected to restart for at least 10 days. Authorities had earlier tried to raise water flow by sinking barges loaded with rocks in the river. The first reactor had already been shut in July; the plant had previously only been shut once, in 2003.

Neighbouring Hungary has so far avoided a shutdown of its Soviet-era Paks plant, which also draws on the Danube, though Prime Minister Péter Magyar warned last month it could be forced to close entirely for the first time. Waters in Europe's second-longest river have fallen to their lowest levels in 30 years in several countries, and the Rhine is also severely limiting traffic. Italy's largest farm association, Coldiretti, said climate-related damage could exceed 3 billion euros.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe's drought is now forcing a nuclear plant offline for cooling-water shortages, exposing how vulnerable the continent's energy system is to climate-driven heat at a time of already-high power prices and tight supply.

sections.heading: Japan's Record Rainfall Kills Four as Russia's Putin Makes First-Ever Kuril Visit
sections.body:
Record rainfall in Japan's Chiba prefecture has killed four people and left thousands stranded overnight at Tokyo's Narita airport, with the meteorological agency issuing a Level 5 Emergency Warning, its highest, before downgrading it to Level 4, the BBC reported. Chiba has recorded more than 100mm of rain per hour since Thursday afternoon, about three times the August average and the highest volume ever recorded in the country. Power was cut to more than 20,000 households, rail and bus services halted, and the Self-Defence Forces were deployed to move people stranded at railway stations.

Separately, President Vladimir Putin made his first-ever visit to the Kuril Islands, meeting the regional governor and touring a fish-processing plant, hospital and school on the southernmost isle of Iturup, according to Russian state media and Al Jazeera. Japan, which claims the four southernmost islands as its Northern Territories, saw Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi call the visit 'absolutely unacceptable', saying it 'offends the sentiments of the Japanese people'.
sections.whyItMatters: An unprecedented rainfall event tests Japan's disaster response and infrastructure just as Tokyo faces a fresh territorial provocation from Moscow, adding friction to an already strained Japan-Russia relationship.

sections.heading: Lebanese Americans Sue US Government and Contractors Over Lebanon War Abuses
sections.body:
Dozens of Lebanese Americans filed a class action lawsuit in the US District Court in Michigan against the US government and defence contractors, alleging their role in Israel's war in Lebanon violates the Leahy Law, which bars assistance to foreign militaries credibly linked to gross human rights abuses, according to Al Jazeera. The suit names Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Lockheed Martin, Boeing and Caterpillar as defendants, and is brought by the Arab American Civil Rights League and 16 individuals, including Michigan businessman Nasser Beydoun, who alleges Israeli forces destroyed his family home in Bint Jbeil 'without any military necessity or justification'.

The plaintiffs argue that by supplying Israel with funds and weapons used in this manner, the US government runs afoul of the Leahy Law. The case comes days after Lebanon passed a long-sought amnesty law and repealed capital punishment, part of a broader post-war reckoning in the country.
sections.whyItMatters: A US court challenge to Washington's weapons pipeline to Israel gives the Lebanon war a legal dimension that could echo in Congress, where scrutiny of arms transfers has already been growing.

sections.heading: Houthi Escalation and Hormuz Claims Keep Middle East Fronts in Motion
sections.body:
Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera warn that a series of Houthi attacks in recent weeks, among the deadliest in years, is raising fears Yemen could slide back towards all-out war as the conflict spreads across the Middle East. The Houthis have killed civilians in attacks on the government-held port of al-Makha, struck Yemeni government military sites in the east killing at least 30 soldiers, and hit Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery. Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council chairman Rashad al-Alimi said the government would not accept 'a new truce that reproduces previous' failures.

On the Strait of Hormuz, Iran reiterated on Thursday that it has full control of the waterway and rejected President Donald Trump's claim of US dominance, according to Al Jazeera. The exchange keeps the standoff at a familiar impasse even as shipping traffic through the strait remains a fraction of its pre-war level.
sections.whyItMatters: The Red Sea front and the Hormuz standoff remain unresolved backdrops to the day's bigger stories, with Houthi attacks threatening to reignite Yemen's civil war and the strait's closure still weighing on global energy markets.

bottomLine: The day's defining story is not a new strike but the mounting human and environmental toll of the wars and crises already underway: a carrier crew at the breaking point after 250-plus days at sea is fuelling Senate pressure on the White House over the Iran war, an 800,000-barrel sanctioned-oil spill is reaching Oman's coast, and Europe's record drought has forced Romania to take its only nuclear plant offline. Japan's unprecedented rainfall and Putin's first-ever Kuril visit add separate strains in Asia. The common thread is that the costs of a prolonged conflict and a warming climate are accumulating faster than leaders can manage them, and the political fallout is beginning to land on those who started them.
